## The Signal Is Real, But It Is Not the Whole Story

The bookmarked post points to a classic small-cap investing pattern: a person with credible industry experience appears to validate a thesis, and the market tries to turn that signal into a shortcut. In this case, the person is Anders Storm, former CEO of Sivers Semiconductors, and the companies are Sivers and POET Technologies, two names tied to the fast-moving world of AI photonics.

The verified part matters. Storm really did run Sivers. The company announced his resignation on March 26, 2024, after roughly a decade in leadership roles, and Sivers later named Vickram Vathulya as president and CEO effective August 19, 2024. Sivers’ own annual report described Storm as CEO since August 2016 and COO before that, with prior experience at Sony Ericsson, HIQ, ABB, and Birdstep. That is meaningful context: he is not a random social-media commentator discovering photonics during an AI rally.

But the post’s second factual hook is weaker. I could not verify from reputable public sources that Storm personally owns POET shares. That does not mean he does not; it means the claim should not be treated as established without a filing, broker disclosure, or direct verifiable statement. In markets, that distinction is not pedantic. Unverified ownership claims can become social proof, and social proof can become price action before the underlying facts catch up.

## Why Sivers And POET Became Linked

The business link between Sivers and POET is real. In September and November 2025, the companies announced a strategic collaboration to combine Sivers’ distributed feedback laser technology with POET’s Optical Interposer platform. The aim is to build external light source modules and light-engine subsystems for co-packaged optics and next-generation AI infrastructure. The companies said prototypes were expected to be shown to customers in the first half of 2026, with production readiness targeted by the end of 2026.

That is the core industrial thesis: AI clusters need faster, lower-power data movement, and optical connectivity is moving deeper into the compute stack. Marvell’s acquisition of Celestial AI, completed on February 2, 2026, reinforced the theme. Marvell said Celestial’s optical interconnect technology could support scale-up connectivity for large AI deployments and projected initial revenue contribution in the second half of fiscal 2028, ramping toward a $500 million annualized run rate in fiscal 2028 and $1 billion in fiscal 2029.

Those are large numbers, and they help explain why investors are hunting upstream suppliers. If optical interconnect becomes a bottleneck, lasers, interposers, packaging, and validated manufacturing capacity all become strategically important.

## The Hard Part: Mapping A Supply Chain Is Not The Same As Owning Revenue

The temptation is to draw a chain: Sivers supplies laser technology to POET; POET has worked with Celestial AI; Celestial is now part of Marvell; Marvell serves major AI infrastructure customers. Each link may be directionally interesting. But a linked ecosystem is not the same as a purchase order, and a purchase order is not the same as durable revenue.

That caution became concrete on April 27, 2026, when POET announced that Marvell Semiconductor, after acquiring Celestial AI, had canceled all purchase orders POET had received from Celestial AI. POET said Marvell cited alleged confidentiality breaches related to the purchase order and shipping information. The episode is a reminder that in strategic hardware markets, commercial relationships can be conditional, confidential, and fragile.

It also illustrates why expert commentary can be most useful as a map, not as a verdict. Someone like Storm may understand the technical architecture, the role of lasers, and the credibility of various product paths. But public investors still need to separate four things: technology feasibility, customer qualification, purchase commitments, and recognized revenue. The market often compresses those stages into a single story. Companies have to pass through them one by one.

## Why It Matters

AI photonics is important because the scaling problem is real. More accelerators create more data movement, and electrical interconnects face power, reach, and bandwidth constraints. Optical approaches, including co-packaged optics and external light sources, are credible answers to those constraints. That makes companies like Sivers and POET worth watching.

The better takeaway from the bookmark is not “follow the ex-CEO.” It is: experienced operators can point investors toward technically meaningful bottlenecks, but the investable claim still depends on evidence. In this corner of the market, the evidence to watch is boring by design: named customers, qualification milestones, production readiness, repeat orders, gross margin, and whether prototypes become shipped products.

The story is not invalid because it spread on X. It is also not validated because it spread on X. The useful posture is to treat the post as a lead, then demand the same proof you would demand from any other supply-chain thesis.

## The Useful Failure of Black-Scholes

Black-Scholes is one of finance’s most productive wrong ideas. In its clean textbook form, the model says that an option’s price can be derived from a few inputs: the underlying price, strike, time to expiration, interest rate, and a single volatility number. That last phrase is where reality starts to push back. If the model were literally right, options on the same asset with the same expiration would imply the same volatility across strikes.

They do not. Market prices usually imply a curve: lower volatility near the money, higher volatility in the wings, or in equity markets a pronounced downside skew where out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility. This is the volatility smile or smirk. It is not a minor cosmetic error. It is the market saying that tail risk, demand for protection, jumps, stochastic volatility, liquidity, and positioning matter.

Yet the model remains everywhere because it is more than a pricing formula. It is a language.

## A Coordinate System, Not a Map

The most practical use of Black-Scholes today is often backward. Traders do not necessarily begin with a volatility estimate and produce a price. They observe a market price and solve the formula for the volatility number that would make Black-Scholes match it. That number, implied volatility, lets traders compare options across strikes, maturities, and underlyings in a compact way.

This is why a flawed model can become infrastructure. Dollars are awkward because every contract has its own strike, tenor, and payoff geometry. Implied volatility normalizes those differences into a market dialect: this strike is rich, that maturity is cheap, the downside wing is bid, the term structure is steep.

The original post’s most interesting frame is geometric. It suggests that Black-Scholes is the flat limit of a more general curved pricing space, and that the volatility smile is the visible sign of that curvature. As a metaphor, this is powerful. In a flat world, one volatility number works everywhere. In a curved world, moving across strikes and maturities changes the local measurement of risk. The surface bends.

But as a factual claim, the geometric version needs more care. The broad phenomenon is verified: Black-Scholes does not predict the observed smile, and researchers have documented systematic relationships between implied volatility, strike, and expiration. The specific claim that a Fisher-information geometry explains the smile as curvature, and that this structure predicts long-dated SPY/VIX skew within about 20% without options calibration, is not established by the sources I could verify. It may be an interesting preprint result; it should not yet be treated as settled market theory.

## Why the Smile Exists

There is no single accepted cause of the smile. Several mechanisms can produce similar shapes.

One explanation is distributional: returns are not lognormal in the neat Black-Scholes sense. Extreme moves happen more often than a thin-tailed model expects, and equity returns are often negatively skewed. Options that pay off in those bad states become more valuable, so their implied volatilities rise.

Another explanation is institutional: demand matters. Portfolio managers buy downside protection. Dealers manage inventory and hedging risk. After the 1987 crash, option markets became far more attentive to crash protection, and equity index skew became a persistent feature. The smile is therefore not simply a forecast of realized volatility; it is also a price of insurance, balance-sheet capacity, and fear.

A third explanation is model-based: stochastic volatility, local volatility, jump diffusion, SABR, Heston, and other frameworks each try to reproduce a surface that Black-Scholes flattens. SABR, for example, became popular because it offered a tractable way to model smile dynamics, especially in rates markets.

The geometric idea belongs in this family of attempts to explain the surface rather than merely fit it. If it works, its value would be conceptual compression: instead of treating the smile as an arbitrary curve to calibrate, it would connect option prices, market dynamics, and information geometry in one structure.

## Why It Matters

The stakes are not academic. A flat volatility assumption underprices some options and overprices others. It can make hedges look cleaner than they are. It can hide exposure to crashes, jumps, and liquidity gaps. A trader who sees only the Black-Scholes price misses the market’s second message: where risk is expensive.

The better lesson is not that Black-Scholes should be discarded. It is that models can be wrong at the level of description and still indispensable at the level of coordination. Black-Scholes gives the market a grammar. The volatility surface supplies the accent, stress, and warning signs.

The post’s frame is useful if read that way. The flat model is the local approximation. The smile is the evidence that the world is not flat. The open question is whether the proposed geometry is merely an elegant metaphor, or a durable predictive theory.

## The Uneasy Message of a Quiet Rally

“The volume is just melting away” is the kind of market comment that sounds simple but carries a large implication. If prices are rising while fewer shares are changing hands, the rally may be getting easier to move but harder to trust. The point is not that low volume predicts an immediate reversal. It is that price without participation tells a less complete story.

That distinction matters because the April 27, 2026 market backdrop was already strange. The S&P 500 closed at 7,173.91, up 0.12%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.20% to 24,887.10, both record closes according to AP and other market reports. Yet Reuters, carried by The Straits Times, described the session as muted, with the major indexes wavering through the day and investors facing a heavy week of earnings, economic data, central-bank decisions, and Middle East risk.

So the seed idea is useful: a record high reached with hesitant participation should be read differently from a record high reached with broad, aggressive demand.

## What Volume Actually Tells You

Volume is often treated as a confirmation tool. Price says where the market went; volume helps describe how much conviction accompanied the move. The CMT Association frames volume as market participation: when price rises on strong volume, more participants appear to be involved in the advance; when price rises on fading volume, the move may be more fragile or more dependent on a smaller set of buyers.

This is especially important near highs. A market can grind upward on declining volume for longer than skeptics expect, because fewer sellers can be enough to lift prices if liquidity is thin. But that same thinness can create air pockets. If a negative catalyst appears, there may be fewer committed buyers underneath the market than the index level implied.

A quiet rally is therefore not bearish by itself. It is a warning to ask better questions: Is leadership broadening or narrowing? Are institutions adding risk or waiting? Are options flows and systematic strategies doing more work than fundamental buying? Are investors simply pausing before earnings?

## The April 2026 Context

The replies to the bookmark captured that tension well. One user argued that “no one is positioning” because of major earnings uncertainty later in the week. Another saw the pattern as a potential bull trap: “all price no volume.” Others were less alarmed, suggesting the volume that did exist still showed reasonable conviction.

The cautious interpretation has support. Reuters described the April 27 session as lacking strong directional conviction, and Barron's noted that the S&P 500 and Nasdaq “barely” reached fresh records, helped by anticipation around Big Tech earnings. That is a very different setup from a broad risk-on surge.

But the stronger version of the claim is harder to validate. Official market-wide volume data available from Nasdaq Trader and Cboe do not show an obvious, verified collapse in trading activity across the whole U.S. market. Nasdaq Trader’s daily summary for earlier April showed total Nasdaq-issue volume moving around materially from day to day, not simply falling in a straight line. Cboe’s March 2026 monthly release showed U.S. equities on-exchange matched-share average daily volume at 2.048 billion, up 4.4% from February and up 26.6% from March 2025 for Cboe venues.

That does not disprove the chart in the bookmark. The image may have referred to a specific index ETF, futures contract, exchange, or shorter intraday window. But it does mean the broad claim should be handled carefully: “volume is fading in this chart” is different from “the market is running out of buyers.”

## Why It Matters

Low-volume advances matter because they change the risk profile of a move. In a high-volume breakout, a large number of participants have revealed a willingness to transact at higher prices. That can create psychological and technical support. In a low-volume breakout, prices may still be rising, but the evidence of shared conviction is thinner.

For investors, the practical lesson is not to sell every quiet high. It is to avoid treating index records as self-validating. A record close is a price fact, not a breadth fact, not a positioning fact, and not a liquidity fact.

The next confirmation would come from whether volume expands on further gains, whether more sectors participate, and whether post-earnings reactions are bought rather than faded. If the market keeps making highs while activity, breadth, and leadership weaken, the “melting away” observation becomes more consequential. If volume returns and gains broaden, the quiet session may simply have been pre-event hesitation.

## The Ratio Behind the Claim

The bookmark points to a simple but provocative valuation lens: divide the S&P 500 by M2, the broad U.S. money supply measure that includes currency, checking deposits, savings deposits, small time deposits, and retail money market funds. The intuition is straightforward. A stock index can rise because corporate earnings, margins, and expected cash flows improve. It can also rise because the denominator of money has expanded. SPX/M2 asks whether equities are gaining faster than the pool of broad money.

On the latest available data, the warning is directionally credible. FRED shows the S&P 500 closed at 7,173.91 on April 27, 2026. M2 was reported at $22,686.0 billion for March 2026 in the latest money-supply update. That gives an SPX/M2 ratio of roughly 0.316. The S&P 500's famous dot-com-era closing high was 1,527.46 on March 24, 2000. With M2 then around $4.6-$4.7 trillion, the ratio was roughly 0.33. So the current ratio is not cleanly a new high on this back-of-the-envelope check, but it is close enough to the 2000 zone to make the comparison worth taking seriously.

## What This Lens Gets Right

The useful part of SPX/M2 is that it refuses to look at the stock market in nominal isolation. Since 2020, investors have become more aware that liquidity and money growth can change the apparent meaning of asset-price records. A 7,000 S&P 500 does not mean the same thing under a $15 trillion M2 regime as it does under a $22 trillion M2 regime.

That matters because many market arguments quietly mix real and nominal claims. Bulls may say the index is at record highs because the U.S. corporate sector is more profitable, asset-light, globally dominant, and AI-levered than it was in 2000. Bears may answer that the price level is being flattered by years of monetary expansion, fiscal deficits, and liquidity preference for large-cap equities. SPX/M2 does not settle that debate, but it gives both sides a common measuring stick.

A high ratio says equities have outrun broad money. That can mean genuine productive strength: companies are converting capital into earnings more efficiently, and investors are paying up for that. It can also mean vulnerability: if liquidity growth slows, rates stay restrictive, or earnings disappoint, the equity market has less monetary cushion underneath it.

## Why the Dot-Com Comparison Is Tempting

The dot-com peak is remembered not just for high prices, but for a narrative that made high prices feel rational. In 2000, investors were paying for a future internet economy that was real but over-discounted too early. Today, the analogous narrative is artificial intelligence, platform scale, and capital-light monopoly economics. Again, parts of the story are real. The risk is valuation compression if the timing, margins, or competitive benefits disappoint.

The SPX/M2 ratio is especially useful here because it is not the same as a price-to-earnings ratio. It does not ask whether companies are expensive relative to profits. It asks whether the equity market has become expensive relative to broad money. If both SPX/M2 and traditional valuation measures are stretched, the signal is stronger. If SPX/M2 is high but earnings quality is also much better than in 2000, the signal is more ambiguous.

## The Big Caveat

This ratio should not be treated as a trading model. The reply pointing out the denominator problem is correct: M2 can rise too. If broad money expands while the S&P 500 rises, the ratio can remain stable even during a major bull market. It also mixes a daily numerator with a monthly denominator, so short-term readings can look more precise than they are.

There is also a structural issue. M2 is not the same as market liquidity, margin capacity, fiscal impulse, global dollar liquidity, or risk appetite. It is a broad monetary aggregate, not a complete map of how money reaches financial assets. A high SPX/M2 ratio can persist for years if earnings growth, buybacks, foreign capital flows, or investor concentration support equities.

## Why It Matters

The right takeaway is not simply 'stocks must crash.' It is that the market is again priced in a zone where liquidity-adjusted optimism is elevated. That should change how investors frame risk. At ratios near the dot-com zone, future returns depend more heavily on continued earnings delivery, benign liquidity conditions, and confidence in the dominant growth story. If any of those weaken, valuation has less room to absorb the shock.

The ratio is a warning light, not a verdict. But warning lights are useful precisely because they appear before the engine fails.

claim_check.claim: The S&P 500 relative to M2 money supply is back near its dot-com bubble high.
claim_check.evidence: Using FRED's latest S&P 500 close of 7,173.91 on April 27, 2026 and the March 2026 M2 figure of $22,686.0 billion reported from FRED, SPX/M2 is about 0.316. The S&P 500's dot-com-era record close was 1,527.46 on March 24, 2000; using historical M2 around $4.6-$4.7 trillion for that period puts the ratio around 0.33. That makes today's reading close to, though not clearly above, the dot-com peak. The comparison is sensitive to daily-vs-monthly timing and the exact M2 observation used.

counterpoints: SPX/M2 is a crude ratio and not a complete valuation model.
M2 is monthly while the S&P 500 is daily, so exact point-in-time comparisons are noisy.
Today's index composition, profitability, buyback activity, and global revenue mix differ significantly from the dot-com era.
A rising M2 denominator could allow stocks to rise further without the ratio breaking materially higher.
2048846490785792133.dek: Comparing the S&P 500 with M2 money supply is an imperfect but useful way to ask whether stocks are outrunning the liquidity backdrop.
2048846490785792133.headline: A Bubble-Era Valuation Gauge Is Flashing Again
implications: The S&P 500 is not merely high in nominal terms; it is also high relative to broad U.S. money supply.
Liquidity-adjusted valuation pressure makes earnings growth, margins, and AI-related capital returns more important to justify current prices.
If M2 growth slows or reverses while equities remain elevated, the ratio could become more stretched even without a dramatic index rally.
The comparison strengthens the case for watching liquidity and valuation together rather than treating stock records as self-explanatory.
media_notes: The attached image likely supplied the visual basis for the SPX/M2 comparison, but the captured media had only generic alt text, so the article relies on independently checked source data rather than details inferred from the image.
questions_to_watch: Does M2 keep growing through 2026, or does liquidity flatten again?
Do S&P 500 earnings revisions support the index level, especially among mega-cap technology firms?
Does the SPX/M2 ratio decisively exceed the 2000 zone or stall below it?
Are other valuation measures, such as forward P/E, CAPE, equity risk premium, and market cap to GDP, confirming the same signal?

reply_context.summary: Replies mainly debated whether the ratio is statistically reliable and whether a rising M2 denominator could let SPY keep rising. The author agreed that the denominator matters while still framing the setup as bearish or at least risky.
useful_signals: One reply cautioned that there are not enough historical occurrences to validate a strong trading rule.
Several replies treated the chart as a risk signal rather than a precise timing tool.
The author suggested a bearish bias toward lower SPX levels but allowed for rallies along the way.
